abstract: The role of social media, in particular microblogging platforms such as Twitter, as a conduit for actionable and tactical information during disasters is increasingly acknowledged. However, time-critical analysis of big crisis data on social media streams brings challenges to machine learning techniques, especially the ones that use supervised learning. The scarcity of labeled data, particularly in the early hours of a crisis, delays the learning process. Existing classification methods require a significant amount of labeled data specific to a particular event for training plus a lot of feature engineering to achieve best results. In this work, we introduce neural network based classification methods for identifying useful tweets during a crisis situation. At the onset of a disaster when no labeled data is available, our proposed method makes the best use of the out-of-event data and achieves good results.

bibliographic.title: Robust Classification of Crisis-Related Data on Social Networks Using Convolutional Neural Networks
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the Eleventh International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2017)

content.problem: Supervised classifiers for detecting useful crisis tweets need event-specific labeled data, which is scarce in the early hours of a disaster when it is needed most.
content.proposed_solution: The authors classify tweets with a convolutional neural network that learns features from word embeddings and can reuse labeled data from past crises when new event labels are missing.
dataset_testbed: CrisisNLP dataset of human-labeled crisis tweets
CrisisLex dataset of human-labeled crisis tweets
AIDR dataset of volunteer-labeled crisis tweets
Crisis embeddings trained with word2vec skip-gram on 57,908 disaster tweets

content.claim: Convolutional neural networks classified crisis tweets more reliably than non-neural classifiers in all training settings and gave reasonable predictions from out-of-event data when no event labels existed.
author_stated_limitations: Classifier performance degraded when out-of-event training samples were added to event-specific data.
